items.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: I feel like I knew Bix Beiderbecke personally and he died in 1931. And I wasn’t born until 1941.

ctx.x: Okay. Is the music that John Coltrane did more of an art form than the music of Bix Beiderbecke?

I think it’s different music but not more of an art form. I don’t think music gets more artistic than Bix Beiderbecke. I don’t think any art gets — I think it’s the consummate art. It think Beiderbecke is the — I mean he is the great American artist. I mean you put him up on the wall. I don’t think it gets, I don’t think art gets any finer.

I’m not sure that I picked the right person, but I sort of get the impression, what we were talking about this morning about where traditional jazz fits in the music scene today and in the IAJE. And somehow I personally get the impression that people don’t think of the music from the 1920s and 30s as artistic as they do jazz from the bop period on. Is it that it became, like because the music was too much of an entertainment type thing?
